title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
extended_summary:
This paper examines how secondary English-as-a-foreign-language students use and edit AI-generated text while composing expository writing. The central research questions are what kinds of edits students make to AI-generated text and what broader patterns characterize their writing processes when working with generative AI. The study is motivated by concern that students may simply paste AI output with little cognitive effort, and by the lack of fine-grained evidence about what students actually do during AI-assisted writing.

The intervention was an AI-assisted writing workshop in which students received instruction on either process-based or genre-based writing, along with prompt engineering for generative AI tools. Students then used the POE app to access chatbots and wrote a 500-word expository article in Google Docs, highlighting AI-generated text and recording their screens. The researchers analyzed 25 usable screen recordings from 29 recruited students using a mixed-methods design combining content analysis, descriptive statistics, thematic analysis, and multiple case studies.

Participants were secondary students in Hong Kong from seven schools, spanning a range of academic achievement levels and grade levels one through five, with ages 12 to 18. The context was a two-hour workshop conducted at schools, with teachers helping recruit students, arrange venues and hardware, and choose an instructional orientation, while the first author delivered the workshop. The study focused on the writing process itself rather than externally measured literacy outcomes.

The authors identified 15 types of AI-generated text edits across seven categories, including insertions, deletions, replacements, formatting actions, and unanticipated AI-initiated edits from Apple iOS predictive text and Google Docs suggestions. They also identified four writing patterns: planning with top-down drafting and revising, top-down drafting and revising without planning, planning with bottom-up drafting and revising, and bottom-up drafting and revising without planning. The paper concludes that students' AI-assisted writing behavior is more active and cognitively complex than simple copy-pasting, but that the Hong Kong EFL context, small sample, and brief single-instance recordings limit generalization.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory mixed-methods study with clear methods and direct K-12 relevance, but it is primarily qualitative/descriptive, lacks a control group, and does not estimate causal effects on literacy outcomes. It therefore fits yellow-tier evidence under the framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides useful but indirect evidence of process-level engagement with generative AI in secondary EFL writing, not quantified impact on learning outcomes. Because outcome effects are unclear and no effect sizes are reported, the impact tier is best classified as yellow.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI-assisted EFL secondary composition writing, focused on how students insert, edit, replace, and delete AI-generated text while drafting and revising expository essays using chatbots and embedded writing suggestions.
Students used POE-accessed chatbots such as ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini to generate ideas, plans, model text, sections, and revisions during machine-in-the-loop writing.

finding.finding_summary: This exploratory mixed-methods study of 25 analyzable Hong Kong secondary EFL screen recordings (from 29 recruited students) found extensive AI-supported writing-process activity, identifying 266 edits across 15 edit types and 7 categories. However, it did not directly measure externally assessed literacy gains, rubric-scored final writing quality, revision quality, or error reduction; the empirical contribution is therefore mainly descriptive process evidence showing students actively modified AI output rather than passively inserting it. No effect sizes or confidence intervals were reported.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded writing-process behaviors; frequencies and categories of AI-generated text insertions, deletions, replacements, and editing patterns during expository composition

finding.finding_summary: The authors interpret the observed editing behaviors as evidence of complex cognitive engagement, planning, and agency management in machine-in-the-loop writing. Four writing-process patterns were identified—planning with top-down drafting/revising (n=1), top-down without planning (n=6), planning with bottom-up drafting/revising (n=15 as reported in text/table, though one subsection says n=13), and bottom-up without planning (n=3)—but these are descriptive patterns rather than validated gains in transferable metacognition or independent performance. No standardized durable-skills outcomes or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative/thematic coding of planning, drafting, revising, and editing-pattern behaviors from screen recordings
